title: {rival} starts a price war
text: {rival} has cut prices by a fifth in {city} and is telling your customers about it, one by one.

opts.label: Match them
opts.hint: Cut your prices 12% across the region. Keeps customers, costs margin, and they will see it as escalation.

out.text: You match. Margins bleed on both sides.

opts.label: Differentiate
opts.hint: Spend on service and marketing instead of price.

out.text: You sell on quality while they sell on price.

opts.label: Hit their home market
opts.hint: Open a second front where it hurts them.

out.text: You undercut them on their own turf. They notice.

opts.label: File a predatory-pricing complaint
opts.hint: Cheap, slow, and usually goes nowhere.

out.text: The regulator orders them to stop.
The complaint is filed and forgotten.

opts.label: Hold your price
opts.hint: Let them burn money.

out.text: You hold. Watch your share in {city} over the next quarters.

lesson: In a price war the winner is whoever has the lowest costs and the deepest pockets. If that is not you, compete on something else — or make peace.

title: {rival} hits back
text: You went after {rival}. Now they have come for you: prices slashed in {city}, your home market, and a sales team with your customer list.

opts.label: Stand firm
opts.hint: Defend the home market on service.

opts.label: Offer a truce
opts.hint: A payment and a handshake.

out.text: {rivalCeo} takes the meeting and declines the truce.

opts.label: Escalate
opts.hint: Match their prices and go after their people.

out.text: It gets worse before it gets better.

lesson: Aggression invites retaliation, usually where you are most exposed. Before attacking a rival, ask what they can do to your home market.

title: {rival} is hiring your people
text: Recruiters working for {rival} have approached a dozen of your best in {city}, with offers a third above what you pay.

opts.label: Counter-offer
opts.hint: Match the money for the ones who matter.

out.text: Most stay. Your wage bill does not.

opts.label: Poach back
opts.hint: Two can play.

out.text: You hire two of theirs. This is now a feud.

opts.label: Enforce the non-competes
opts.hint: Lawyers’ letters to everyone who leaves.

out.text: They leave anyway, and the letters are read out at their leaving drinks.

opts.label: Let them go
opts.hint: Anyone who leaves for money was going to leave.

lesson: Talent raids target companies that pay below market or treat people as replaceable. The defence is built before the recruiters call.

title: {rival} sues you
text: {rival} has filed a patent suit claiming your core product infringes three of its patents. They want an injunction.

opts.label: Settle
opts.hint: Pay a licence fee and move on.

opts.label: Fight it
opts.hint: Their patents look weak.

out.text: The court agrees the patents are weak.

opts.label: Counter-sue
opts.hint: You have patents too.

out.text: They drop the suit rather than risk yours.
Both suits grind on. Only the lawyers win.

lesson: Litigation is a competitive weapon: it costs the defendant management attention even when the case is weak. A patent portfolio is as much deterrent as protection.

title: New rules, conveniently shaped
text: {rival} has been lobbying for new regulations in {region}. The draft happens to exempt companies exactly like {rival}.

opts.label: Counter-lobby
opts.hint: Hire people who know the committee.

opts.label: Comply early and say so
opts.hint: Turn the cost into a selling point.

out.text: You are first to be certified.

opts.label: Ignore it
opts.hint: Regulations take years.

lesson: Regulation is a competitive arena. Incumbents use rules to raise rivals’ costs; being absent from the room is itself a decision.

title: Whispers
text: Customers keep asking whether it is true that you are running out of money. The rumour traces back to {rival}’s sales team.

opts.label: Answer with facts
opts.hint: Publish your numbers and call key customers.

out.text: Denials keep it alive a little longer.

opts.label: Ignore it
opts.hint: Do not dignify it.

opts.label: Retaliate in kind
opts.hint: You know things about them too.

out.text: Now both of you look bad.

lesson: A company’s perceived stability is part of its product, especially when customers depend on you for years. Reputation and a visible cash cushion are the defence.

title: {rival} locks up your supplier
text: Your main supplier in {region} has signed an exclusive with {rival}. Your contract ends next quarter.

opts.label: Find another source
opts.hint: Requalify in a hurry.

out.text: A scramble, and higher costs for a year.

opts.label: Outbid them
opts.hint: Pay to break the exclusive.

out.text: The supplier discovers it has two customers after all.

opts.label: Sue for interference
opts.hint: Your contract had a renewal clause.

lesson: A single source of supply is a lever for anyone who wants to hurt you. Dual sourcing costs a little every year and saves a lot once.

title: {rival} has cloned your product
text: A new release from {rival} looks remarkably like yours, down to the wording in the menus.

opts.label: Sue
opts.hint: It is blatant.

out.text: Look-and-feel is hard to protect. You lose.

opts.label: Out-innovate them
opts.hint: By the time they copy this version, ship the next.

opts.label: Shrug
opts.hint: Imitation is flattery.

lesson: A lead that can be copied is temporary. Durable advantage comes from things that are slow to imitate: scale, brand, relationships, and the pace of improvement itself.

title: {rival} is courting {person}
text: {rivalCeo} has taken {person}, your {role}, to dinner twice this month.

opts.label: Match whatever they offer
opts.hint: Money and a new title.

opts.label: Let them choose
opts.hint: If they want to go, they should go.

out.text: {person} stays, and tells you about the offer.

opts.label: Call {rivalCeo}
opts.hint: A frank conversation between chief executives.

out.text: An awkward call. They back off, for now.

lesson: Your key people are known to your rivals. Loyalty is built from pay, respect and prospects long before the dinner invitations arrive.

title: {rivalCeo} takes a swing
text: On stage at an industry event, {rivalCeo} described your company as "a nice little business, for now". The clip is everywhere.

opts.label: Reply in kind
opts.hint: You have a few lines of your own.

out.text: The feud is good for both brands and bad for relations.

opts.label: Stay classy
opts.hint: Say something gracious.

opts.label: Put it on a billboard
opts.hint: Quote them in your advertising.

out.text: "A nice little business" becomes your slogan for a season.

lesson: Being attacked by a larger rival is free publicity. How you answer says more about you than what they said.

title: {rival} opens in {city}
text: {rival} has taken office space three streets from your headquarters. Their opening party is on Thursday.

opts.label: Cut prices before they land
opts.hint: Make the market unattractive.

out.text: You welcome them with a price cut.

opts.label: Lock in your customers
opts.hint: Long contracts at a small discount.

out.text: Most of your base signs up before the party.

opts.label: Do nothing
opts.hint: Competition is normal.

lesson: An entrant starts with no customers and a liability of newness. Your advantage is incumbency; how much of your margin you spend defending it is the question.

title: {rival} is in trouble
text: {rival} has missed a loan payment and its suppliers are demanding cash up front. Its people are polishing their CVs.

opts.label: Buy their {city} operation
opts.hint: Pay cash for the office, its customers and its staff.

out.text: The administrator is happy to deal.

opts.label: Hire their best people
opts.hint: Experienced staff, no recruiter fees.

opts.label: Go after their customers
opts.hint: Tell the market what you know.

opts.label: Watch
opts.hint: Let events take their course.

lesson: A competitor’s distress is the cheapest growth available — to those with cash on hand when it happens. This is what a strong balance sheet is for.

title: {rival} proposes a truce
text: {rivalCeo} has asked to meet. "This is costing us both money," the note says.

opts.label: Accept
opts.hint: Two years of peace.

opts.label: Accept, if they leave {city}
opts.hint: Press the advantage.

opts.label: Refuse
opts.hint: You are winning.

lesson: A war that both sides are losing can only be ended by one of them offering peace. Whether to accept depends on whose position is improving.

title: {rival} proposes an alliance
text: {rivalCeo} suggests working together: joint marketing in the markets you share, and a common front against the others.

opts.label: Sign
opts.hint: Three years. Shared marketing, shared information.

opts.label: Try a small pilot
opts.hint: One campaign, then see.

out.text: A modest joint campaign, and a little more trust.

opts.label: Decline
opts.hint: You do not share customers with competitors.

lesson: Alliances between competitors are unstable: each partner is tempted to learn more than it teaches. Know what you are giving them access to.

title: Your ally has been taking notes
text: Customers report that {rival} is using what it learned in your alliance to pitch them directly.

opts.label: End the alliance
opts.hint: And say why.

opts.label: Confront them privately
opts.hint: Give them a chance to stop.

out.text: They deny it and carry on.

lesson: Trust in a competitor is a position, and positions can lose money.

title: A quiet word
text: Over coffee, {rivalCeo} suggests that you both "stop being silly about prices". Nothing in writing, of course.

opts.label: Agree, quietly
opts.hint: Prices up 8% on both sides. Illegal almost everywhere.

opts.label: Decline politely
opts.hint: Change the subject.

opts.label: Report it
opts.hint: The competition authority has a hotline.

out.text: {rival} is investigated and fined. They know who called.

lesson: Price-fixing is the most tempting crime in business because both sides profit and the victim is diffuse. It is also the one regulators reward your co-conspirator for reporting.

title: Dawn raid
text: Investigators arrived at seven this morning with a warrant covering all pricing communications for the last two years.

opts.label: Confess first
opts.hint: Apply for leniency before {rival} does.

opts.label: Deny everything
opts.hint: There was nothing in writing.

out.text: They find nothing they can use.
{rival} confessed first. You take the full penalty.

lesson: Leniency programmes make cartels a prisoner’s dilemma: the first to confess walks, and everyone knows it.

title: {rival} wants to buy you
text: {rivalCeo} has made a written offer for the whole company: {amount}, cash. Your investors have seen it.

opts.label: Sell
opts.hint: Take the money. The game ends here.

opts.label: Refuse
opts.hint: Not for sale.

opts.label: Propose a partnership instead
opts.hint: There may be a deal short of a sale.

out.text: They agree to a truce and a joint venture.
They wanted the company, not a friend.

lesson: An offer for the company puts a price on the alternative to everything you are planning. Sometimes the right answer is yes.

title: Hostile bid
text: {rival} has gone over your head to shareholders with an offer of {amount} for the company. You own less than half the votes.

opts.label: Poison pill
opts.hint: Lawyers, bankers and a rights plan.

opts.label: Find a white knight
opts.hint: Sell 15% to a friendly investor who will vote with you.

out.text: The friendly block defeats the bid.

opts.label: Buy back shares
opts.hint: Shrink the float and raise your own stake.

out.text: The buyback lifts the price above the bid.

opts.label: Recommend the offer
opts.hint: Take the premium. The game ends here.

lesson: Once you sell more than half the company you are an employee of the shareholders. A depressed share price and a low founder stake are an invitation.

title: A merger of equals
text: {rivalCeo} proposes combining {rival} with your company. You would be chief executive; their shareholders would own a share in proportion to value.

opts.label: Merge
opts.hint: One company, twice the size, two cultures.

out.text: The merger completes. Now comes the hard part.

opts.label: Decline
opts.hint: You would rather compete.

lesson: Mergers of equals double scale overnight and usually take years to integrate. Most of the value is lost in culture, not strategy.

title: Verdict
text: The court has ruled on your suit against {rival}.

opts.label: Read the judgment
opts.hint: Litigation is uncertain.

out.text: You win. {rival} pays damages and changes its product.
You lose, and pay their costs.

lesson: A lawsuit is an investment with a binary payoff and a certain cost. File when the odds and the stakes justify it, not when you are angry.
